items.q: A 75-year-old male with severe aortic stenosis is evaluated. Echo shows mean gradient 35 mmHg, Vmax 3.8 m/s, AVA 0.9 cm2, and LVEF 45%. Stroke volume index is 30 mL/m2. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
items.exp: Dobutamine stress echo helps distinguish true severe AS in LVEF below 50 percent with flow reserve.
r: Calcium scoring is primarily used for discordant echo findings in preserved ejection fraction AS.
Pseudo-severe AS needs to be excluded before proceeding to definitive surgical or transcatheter intervention.
Exercise testing is generally contraindicated or less useful in patients with severely reduced LVEF.
Dobutamine stress echo helps distinguish true severe AS in LVEF below 50 percent with flow reserve.
items.kp: In low-flow low-gradient AS with LVEF below 50 percent, dobutamine stress echo with 20 percent flow reserve identifies true severe AS.

items.q: A 72-year-old male with severe asymptomatic aortic stenosis is under active surveillance. He asks how frequently he should be evaluated in the clinic to ensure his condition is monitored appropriately. What is the standard recommendation?
items.exp: Guidelines mandate at least 6-monthly reviews to assess symptoms and echo parameters in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
r: Guidelines mandate at least 6-monthly reviews to assess symptoms and echo parameters in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis.
Surveillance interval is too long for severe disease, risking delayed intervention for symptom onset.
More frequent than the recommended 6-monthly intervals for asymptomatic patients.
This interval is insufficient for managing severe aortic stenosis monitoring.
items.kp: Asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis require clinical and echocardiographic surveillance at least every 6 months.

items.q: A 68-year-old female undergoes successful TAVI for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. She has no atrial fibrillation or other indications for chronic anticoagulation. What is the optimal long-term antiplatelet therapy for this patient?
items.exp: Patients without anticoagulation indications receive daily aspirin for 12 months post-TAVI.
r: Aggressive dual antiplatelet therapy increases bleeding risk without proven benefit in this group.
Anticoagulation is only indicated if there is another underlying indication, not for TAVI alone.
Current recommendations favor aspirin monotherapy for patients without specific anticoagulation indications.
Patients without anticoagulation indications receive daily aspirin for 12 months post-TAVI.
items.kp: Standard post-TAVI management for those without anticoagulation needs is aspirin 75-100 mg daily for the first year.

items.q: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with severe aortic stenosis and hypertension. He is currently asymptomatic. Which antihypertensive strategy is preferred to manage his blood pressure while minimizing risks?
items.exp: ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred for hypertension in AS, requiring cautious titration to prevent symptomatic hypotension.
r: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are not the first-line preference compared to ACE inhibitors/ARBs in AS.
ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred for hypertension in AS, requiring cautious titration to prevent symptomatic hypotension.
Beta-blockers are not the preferred first-line agents for hypertension specifically in severe AS patients.
Untreated hypertension in severe AS is detrimental and should be managed with specific agents.
items.kp: Hypertension in severe aortic stenosis should be treated with cautious titration of ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

items.q: A 70-year-old patient with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis presents with haemodynamic instability and requires an urgent non-cardiac surgery. What is the most appropriate management for the valvular lesion?
items.exp: Balloon valvotomy serves as a bridge for haemodynamically unstable patients or before urgent non-cardiac procedures.
r: Statins do not slow the progression or provide immediate stabilization of severe aortic stenosis.
Surgical valve replacement is often not feasible or high-risk in the acute unstable setting.
Balloon valvotomy serves as a bridge for haemodynamically unstable patients or before urgent non-cardiac procedures.
Balloon valvotomy is the specific bridge therapy indicated for haemodynamic instability in this context.
items.kp: Balloon aortic valvotomy is a temporizing bridge for unstable patients or pre-urgent non-cardiac surgery.

items.q: A 68-year-old male with a mechanical aortic valve replacement performed 3 months ago presents for a routine dental extraction. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding endocarditis prophylaxis?
o: Recommend antibiotic prophylaxis for the dental procedure.
Order prophylaxis only if the procedure involves deep gingival tissue manipulation.
Only provide prophylaxis if the patient has a history of endocarditis.
Advise the patient that prophylaxis is unnecessary as the valve is mechanical.
items.exp: Prophylaxis is indicated in all patients who have received a valve replacement, including TAVI, for dental procedures.
r: Prophylaxis is indicated in all patients who have received a valve replacement, including TAVI, for dental procedures.
Prophylaxis is standard for any dental procedure manipulating the gingival or periapical region in valve-replaced patients.
Prophylaxis is indicated based on the presence of a prosthetic valve, regardless of prior endocarditis history.
Prophylaxis is explicitly indicated for all patients with prosthetic valves, mechanical or bioprosthetic.
items.kp: Endocarditis prophylaxis is required for all patients with valve replacements before dental procedures involving gingival or periapical manipulation.

items.q: A patient with severe aortic stenosis is scheduled for urgent non-cardiac surgery. During induction of anesthesia, the team must prioritize the prevention of which hemodynamic state?
o: Induction of a dense neuraxial block to ensure adequate analgesia.
Avoidance of abrupt vasodilation and hypotension.
Maintenance of a heart rate exceeding 110 beats per minute.
Strict avoidance of any vasoconstrictor agents during the procedure.
items.exp: Severe AS requires maintaining systemic pressure; hypotension and vasodilation can critically reduce coronary perfusion and cardiac output.
r: Dense neuraxial blocks can cause abrupt vasodilation, which is specifically cautioned against in severe AS management.
Severe AS requires maintaining systemic pressure; hypotension and vasodilation can critically reduce coronary perfusion and cardiac output.
Tachycardia must be avoided as it shortens diastole and increases myocardial oxygen demand, worsening ischemia in AS.
Vasoconstrictors are actually indicated to treat hypotension promptly in patients with severe AS during surgery.
items.kp: Anesthesia for severe AS must avoid hypotension, tachycardia, and abrupt vasodilation to prevent cardiovascular collapse.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman with known severe symptomatic aortic stenosis plans to become pregnant. What is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?
o: Proceed with pregnancy and monitor with monthly echocardiograms.
Perform balloon valvuloplasty only after the first trimester.
Continue medical management and initiate beta-blocker therapy.
Undergo treatment for the aortic stenosis prior to conception.
items.exp: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis should be definitively treated before pregnancy to reduce maternal and fetal risks.
r: Pregnancy in the presence of severe symptomatic AS carries high risk; intervention is required beforehand.
Treatment, such as surgical or transcatheter repair, should be completed before conception rather than during pregnancy.
Medical therapy is insufficient for symptomatic severe AS; pre-conception definitive treatment is the standard of care.
Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis should be definitively treated before pregnancy to reduce maternal and fetal risks.
items.kp: Symptomatic severe AS should be surgically or interventionally treated before attempting pregnancy.

items.q: In a sedentary 70-year-old patient, breathlessness is attributed to deconditioning. What is the best strategy to clarify if the breathlessness is instead due to underlying aortic stenosis?
o: Assume the symptoms are related to the aortic stenosis without further testing.
Schedule a repeat echocardiogram in six months for reassessment.
Utilization of natriuretic peptides or formal exercise testing.
Measure the resting mean gradient and valve area accurately.
items.exp: Natriuretic peptides or exercise testing help distinguish symptomatic cardiac pathology from age-related deconditioning in sedentary patients.
r: Clinical assessment requires objective confirmation with NP or exercise testing to avoid misdiagnosis.
Delaying assessment fails to address the diagnostic uncertainty regarding potentially serious underlying symptomatic AS.
Natriuretic peptides or exercise testing help distinguish symptomatic cardiac pathology from age-related deconditioning in sedentary patients.
Resting parameters may be misleading; provocative testing or biomarkers are needed for symptomatic sedentary patients.
items.kp: For sedentary patients, exercise testing or natriuretic peptides are essential to differentiate AS symptoms from deconditioning.

items.q: When evaluating a patient with low-gradient aortic stenosis, which parameters must be assessed to avoid misclassifying the severity as moderate?
o: BNP levels, right ventricular function, and mitral regurgitation.
Mean gradient, peak velocity, and heart rate.
Symptom status, valve area, and exercise capacity.
Stroke volume index, LVEF, and calcium score.
items.exp: These three specific measures are necessary to properly grade low-gradient AS and avoid diagnostic errors.
r: These parameters are secondary and do not replace the primary requirement for EF, SV index, and calcium score.
These do not adequately distinguish low-gradient severity without functional and structural indices like calcium and EF.
While relevant, clinical guidelines emphasize stroke volume index, LVEF, and calcium score to confirm true severe disease.
These three specific measures are necessary to properly grade low-gradient AS and avoid diagnostic errors.
items.kp: Low-gradient AS requires analysis of stroke volume index, LVEF, and calcium score to confirm true severity.

items.q: A patient returns for follow-up 6 weeks after surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement. What is the required follow-up imaging protocol for this patient?
o: Yearly echocardiographic review only, without the need for periodic clinical assessment.
Baseline echocardiogram is only necessary if the patient develops symptoms.
Establish a baseline echocardiogram and then conduct yearly clinical and echocardiographic reviews.
Follow-up with clinical exams every six months and echocardiogram every three years.
items.exp: Guidelines require a baseline echo shortly after replacement, followed by annual reviews of clinical status and echo findings.
r: Comprehensive review must include both clinical and echocardiographic evaluations annually.
A baseline echocardiogram is mandatory shortly after valve replacement regardless of symptom status.
Guidelines require a baseline echo shortly after replacement, followed by annual reviews of clinical status and echo findings.
Yearly, not three-yearly, echocardiographic assessment is the standard frequency for monitoring bioprosthetic valves.
items.kp: Post-valve replacement requires a baseline echocardiogram shortly after surgery and yearly clinical/echo monitoring.

items.q: A 74-year-old male with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis presents for preoperative evaluation. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. Which therapeutic intervention poses the greatest risk of immediate cardiovascular collapse in this patient?
items.exp: Nitrates reduce preload, which is critical for maintaining cardiac output in fixed outflow obstruction like severe AS.
r: Beta-blockers are generally tolerated in stable AS to control heart rate and symptoms.
Imaging is a diagnostic procedure and does not induce sudden hemodynamic instability.
Nitrates reduce preload, which is critical for maintaining cardiac output in fixed outflow obstruction like severe AS.
Anticoagulation does not acutely alter hemodynamic stability in severe aortic stenosis patients.
items.kp: In severe AS, the heart relies on high filling pressures; vasodilators and diuretics can precipitate sudden, profound hypotension.

items.q: A 68-year-old patient is scheduled for transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis. Besides assessment of the coronary arteries, what specific condition must be screened for to ensure appropriate management and outcome?
items.exp: Guideline-directed screening for amyloidosis is essential as it frequently coexists and complicates aortic valve pathology interventions.
r: Vascular access assessment is standard, but not the specific secondary pathology mentioned in screening guidelines.
While relevant for surgical risk, it is not a specific diagnostic exclusion for valvular intervention.
This is a hemodynamic consequence of valvular disease, not a required pre-intervention screening condition.
Guideline-directed screening for amyloidosis is essential as it frequently coexists and complicates aortic valve pathology interventions.
items.kp: Cardiac amyloidosis and coronary artery disease are critical occult conditions to exclude before treating symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.

items.q: A 68-year-old male with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis presents for management. His echocardiography confirms a mean gradient of 45 mmHg and an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2. His surgical risk score is low, and he has favorable anatomy for a transfemoral approach. Which intervention is the most appropriate recommendation according to the latest ESC/EACTS guidelines?
items.exp: Guidelines recommend SAVR for low-risk symptomatic patients under 70 years of age.
r: Guidelines recommend SAVR for low-risk symptomatic patients under 70 years of age.
Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis requires definitive intervention to improve long-term survival outcomes.
TAVI is typically reserved for patients aged 70 years or older per current guidelines.
Valvuloplasty is a bridge therapy, not the definitive treatment for symptomatic severe disease.
items.kp: The choice between SAVR and TAVI in severe aortic stenosis is primarily age-stratified, with a 70-year threshold for low-surgical-risk patients.

items.q: A 78-year-old male with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis and an LVEF of 35% is scheduled for elective cardiac valve replacement. His STS score is 8%. What is the most appropriate management approach for this high-risk patient?
items.exp: Guidelines mandate a Heart Team decision between TAVI or SAVR for high-risk patients with LV dysfunction.
r: Guidelines mandate a Heart Team decision between TAVI or SAVR for high-risk patients with LV dysfunction.
Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis requires definitive valve intervention, not medical management, in this population.
Individual surgeon preference does not supersede the mandatory multidisciplinary Heart Team consensus requirement.
TAVI is not the default; choice between TAVI and SAVR requires specific multidisciplinary deliberation.
items.kp: For high-risk elective surgical candidates with symptomatic disease or LV dysfunction, the Heart Team must decide between SAVR and TAVI.
